title: Lot's wife looks back (Genesis 19)
hook: the cities fall, and a woman with no name turns to look
tomorrow: hagar and ishmael in the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday: arguing for Sodom, from fifty good people down to ten. Your line was argue for mercy. Did you speak up for someone who wasn't there? Day forty-six.

Two of the travelers reach Sodom at evening. Lot is sitting at the city gate, and like his uncle he jumps up, bows, and brings them home to eat. But that night the men of the city surround the house and demand the strangers be handed over. It's the opposite of Abraham's open tent: a city that turns on its guests. The visitors strike the mob blind, and tell Lot: take your family and get out. This place is about to be destroyed. At dawn, Lot is still dithering. The Torah uses a word for it that sounds like dragging your feet. So the angels simply grab him, his wife and his two daughters by the hand, and pull them out of the city. Run for your life, they say. Don't look back.
screen: `LOT WELCOMES THE STRANGERS.` → `A CITY TURNS ON ITS GUESTS.` → `DON'T LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: Fire and sulfur rain down on Sodom and Gomorrah. And then one sentence, in the old JPS translation: "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt." That's all we're told about her. She has no name in the Torah. We don't hear her say a single word. Later tradition gave her a name, Edit, and the rabbis asked the question the text leaves open: why did she look? One old midrash answers with compassion. Some of her daughters were married and still in the city, and she turned to see whether they were following. A mother looking for her children. Another midrash, cited by Rashi, gives a sharper answer. It says that when Lot brought the guests home, she wouldn't give them even salt for their food, and so she became salt. It ties her to the city's real sin. And that sin, in the Jewish tradition, is cruelty. The prophet Ezekiel describes Sodom as proud and full of bread, living at ease, and never helping the poor and needy. The Talmud tells stories of Sodom's laws against strangers and against charity. So what does looking back mean? Maybe that you can't be rescued from a place while your heart is still living there. Lot dragged his feet. His wife turned around. The story doesn't mock her; it grieves. And today, near the Dead Sea, there's a pillar of rock salt that people call Lot's wife, still standing, still facing the wrong way.
screen: `A PILLAR OF SALT.` · `NO NAME, NO WORDS.` · `LOOKING FOR HER DAUGHTERS?` · `SODOM'S SIN: CRUELTY.` · then, large: `SHE LOOKED BACK FROM BEHIND HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you keep looking back at. An old argument you replay. A job you didn't get. A version of your life that ended. Looking back is human; it can be love, like a mother looking for her daughters. But notice if it's keeping you frozen. Hold that thing gently in your mind. Thank it for what it was. Then, on an out-breath, picture turning your face forward. If you pray, you can ask for help letting go. The bell holds the time.
Lot's wife looks back. A woman with no name, rescued by the hand, who turned toward the burning city and became a pillar of salt.
Your line: face forward. Today, when your mind turns back to that old thing, notice it kindly, and turn your face forward again. Day forty-six.

howItsDone: Jews read the destruction of Sodom in the Torah portion Vayera; rabbinic tradition teaches that Sodom's sin was cruelty to strangers and the poor, and many teachers pair the story with Ezekiel's description of the city.

fork.setup: you're running from the burning city. the angels said, don't look back. behind you, you hear it falling. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Lot's wife looks back from behind him and becomes a pillar of salt. the Torah gives no reason; the midrash imagines she was looking for her daughters.

trapdoor: what you thought: she was punished for being curious.
what it means: a nameless woman, rescued by the hand, turns toward the city her heart hasn't left, and the story grieves her.
what a scholar hears: two midrashim: she looked for her married daughters (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 25), or she refused guests salt (Genesis Rabbah 51:5, via Rashi).

sources.quoted: But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.

notes: Sensitive: the mob scene (19:4–11) is summarized without detail; Lot's offer of his daughters is omitted. Confirm this is acceptable for the path's tone.
Name 'Edit' (Idit) for Lot's wife: from later midrash (e.g. Midrash Tanhuma / Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer traditions). Confirm the source.
PRE 25: she looked back out of pity for her married daughters in Sodom. Confirm.
Salt midrash: Genesis Rabbah 50:4 or 51:5, cited by Rashi on 19:26. Confirm the chapter number.
Ezekiel 16:49 paraphrased; Sanhedrin 109a–b on Sodom's laws. Confirm.
'Lot's wife' salt pillar on Mount Sodom near the Dead Sea: a known formation. Confirm.
